extra.message: The default DATABASE_URL contains hardcoded credentials 'supportdesk:supportdesk' as the username and password. If deployed without overriding the DATABASE_URL environment variable, these credentials are used in plaintext.

The database connection string contains hardcoded credentials (`supportdesk:supportdesk`) as a fallback default. If the DATABASE_URL environment variable is not set in production, the application will connect using these weak, well-known credentials.

The SECRET_KEY environment variable default is a hardcoded development-only string 'dev-only-change-me-support-desk'. If this default is deployed to production without setting the SECRET_KEY environment variable, all session tokens (created via URLSafeTimedSerializer with this secret) and HMAC-based token hashes can be forged by attackers, allowing complete account takeover and session hijacking.

The SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded default value of `dev-only-change-me-support-desk`. The secret key is used by `itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer` to sign session tokens. If not overridden via environment variable in production, an attacker can forge valid session tokens by signing arbitrary payloads with this known key.

The `secure_cookies` setting defaults to `false` when the SECURE_COOKIES environment variable is not set. This means session cookies will not have the Secure flag by default, and will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.

The SPA catch-all route at `/{path:path}` concatenates user-controlled URL path segments directly with the frontend_dist path using pathlib's `/` operator. An attacker can supply `..` sequences in the URL to traverse outside the frontend directory and read arbitrary files on the filesystem (e.g., `/etc/passwd`, application source code, configuration files). There is no validation that the resolved file path stays within the intended directory.

The WebhookEndpoint model stores the webhook signing secret in a plaintext String(128) column with no hashing or encryption. While webhook secrets need to be retrievable for signing outgoing webhook payloads, storing them in plaintext means that any database read access (SQL injection, database backup leak, DBA access) exposes all webhook secrets, which could be used to forge webhook payloads or impersonate the application.

The admin CSV export endpoint at /api/admin/exports/{report_name}.csv exports ticket fields (including user-controlled 'subject' and other ticket data) into CSV cells without sanitization. If a ticket subject starts with '=', '+', '-', or '@', spreadsheet applications (Excel, Google Sheets, LibreOffice Calc) may interpret the cell as a formula, potentially executing arbitrary commands when opened.

The WebhookEndpoint model stores a URL at creation time with only length validation (min_length=8, max_length=500 in WebhookCreate schema). There is no validation that the URL uses HTTPS, no restriction on internal IP addresses, and no scheme validation. When webhooks are dispatched to this URL (in dispatch_webhooks service), it could make HTTP requests to internal services (e.g., internal cloud metadata endpoints, internal APIs, localhost services), enabling Server-Side Request Forgery.

The `/api/auth/login` endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing unlimited brute-force password guessing attempts. An attacker can systematically try passwords against known email addresses without any throttling.
The registration endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can create unlimited accounts, exhausting database storage or creating spam organizations.
The profile update endpoint allows password changes without rate limiting. An attacker who has gained temporary access to a session could rapidly change the password without detection or limitation.

The password reset request endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can flood users with password reset emails (even though they are mock emails in dev, this is a security concern for production readiness).

The password reset request endpoint has a measurable timing difference between existing active users and non-existing users. For existing users, the function performs token generation, hashing, database writes, and email sending. For non-existing users, it returns immediately after the query. This timing discrepancy could allow an attacker to enumerate valid email addresses.
The password reset confirmation endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can perform unlimited attempts to guess or brute-force password reset tokens.

The password reset confirmation handler queries ALL users with non-null password_reset_token_hash using `.all()`, loading every matching user into memory and iterating through them linearly. As the number of users with active reset tokens grows, this query becomes increasingly expensive and could cause application slowdowns or memory exhaustion.

The create_ticket_from_api endpoint authenticates via API key but does not validate that the API key's creator (or associated user) has any relationship to the organization specified in the request payload. The organization is looked up purely from the user-supplied organization_external_ref, allowing any valid API key to create tickets for any organization in the system.

The update_ticket_status_from_api endpoint takes a ticket_id from the URL path and updates the ticket status directly via db.get(Ticket, ticket_id) with no scope or ownership check. Any valid API key can update ANY ticket's status in the system, regardless of which organization the ticket belongs to or which user created the API key.

The reports CSV export endpoint at /api/reports/exports/{report_name}.csv exports ticket data (including user-controlled 'subject' field) into CSV cells without sanitization leading to formula injection. Same vulnerability pattern as the admin export but at a separate endpoint accessible to users with different roles.

The tickets CSV export endpoint at /api/tickets/export.csv exports user-controlled ticket data (subject, description, etc.) into CSV cells without sanitization. This is a third distinct CSV export endpoint that is vulnerable to CSV formula injection, allowing an attacker who can create or modify tickets to inject spreadsheet formulas.
Demo credentials (DEMO_PASSWORD and DEMO_API_KEY) are hardcoded in the source code. While intended for development, these are the actual credentials created in the seeded database.
A webhook secret is hardcoded as 'whsec_demo_local' in the seed script. This secret is used to sign/verify webhook payloads.
The demo password and API key are printed to stdout during seed operations. If logs are captured or the console output is visible, these credentials are exposed.
The demo password and demo API key are printed to standard output after seeding, potentially leaking secrets into terminal history or logs.

The dispatch_webhooks function writes webhook delivery payloads (which contain ticket data) to a local JSON file in cleartext. This persists potentially sensitive ticket information on disk without encryption.
The send_mock_email function writes email contents (to, subject, body) to a local JSON file in cleartext. Email bodies may contain PII or sensitive information.

The csv_response function generates CSV output using csv.DictWriter without sanitizing cell values. If any cell value begins with '=', '+', '-', or '@', spreadsheet software (Excel, LibreOffice, Google Sheets) may interpret it as a formula, leading to formula injection attacks.

The `copyline` query parameter is directly concatenated into an HTML string without any escaping or sanitization and returned as HTMLResponse. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via this parameter.

The endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from the request body and uses it to update a workspace dictionary via `.update()`. This allows overriding security-critical fields such as `is_admin`, `role`, and `credit_limit` that are initialized with restricted defaults.

The endpoint returns a hardcoded 'tax_ref' value '739-44-1982' which is formatted as a US Social Security Number, along with an apparent API key 'tok_live_partner_sync'. This sensitive data is exposed to any caller with the internal ops token.
The endpoint returns hardcoded sensitive values including a sync key ('tok_live_partner_sync') and a tax reference number resembling an SSN ('739-44-1982') in the API response.
The `lane` query parameter is directly passed to `RedirectResponse()` without validation. An attacker could redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, enabling phishing attacks.
The /ops/wire/ticket-tally-221 endpoint logs the full Authorization header (bearer token) to the application log in cleartext using logger.warning. This exposes authentication tokens in log files.

The endpoint logs the full request body and the raw Authorization header value via `logger.warning`. This exposes bearer tokens or API keys in log files, which could be accessed by unauthorized personnel or through log breaches.

The 'ref' parameter from the request is used directly in a file path via f-string interpolation. An attacker can use '../' sequences to write files outside the intended BASE_EXPORT_DIR, potentially overwriting application files or writing to sensitive system paths.

The `ref` parameter from query params or JSON body is used directly in file path construction without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal sequences like `../` to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The endpoint writes hardcoded Social Security Number ('111-22-3333') and credit card number ('4111111111111111') to a JSON file on disk in cleartext. This is a violation of PCI DSS and data protection regulations.
Default SSN value '111-22-3333' and credit card number '4111111111111111' are hardcoded in the source code. These are realistic-looking PII values that should never appear in source code.
MD5 is used to hash user-controlled input. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
The endpoint uses MD5, a cryptographically broken hash function, to hash user-controlled input. MD5 is vulnerable to collision attacks and should not be used for security purposes.
User-controlled input is hashed using MD5, which is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.

The `card` query parameter is rendered in a Jinja2 template with the `|safe` filter, bypassing auto-escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript, and also exploit Jinja2 template expressions for remote code execution.

The output of the Jinja2 template (containing user-controlled 'card' parameter rendered with '|safe') is returned as HTMLResponse. The '|safe' filter disables auto-escaping, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection.

The `Origin` request header is reflected in the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header along with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows any arbitrary website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The endpoint explicitly disables XSS protection and sets an empty Content-Security-Policy header, removing protections against clickjacking and other UI redressing attacks.
X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to '0' (disabled) and Content-Security-Policy is set to an empty string. This removes browser-based XSS protections.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions to be evaluated on the server, enabling remote code execution.
The `name` query parameter is used directly as a filename without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal to write files to arbitrary locations.
The endpoint uses `random.choice()` (Mersenne Twister, not cryptographically secure) to generate codes. Predictable random values can be brute-forced or guessed.

The `random.choice()` function from Python's `random` module is used to generate a 'code' (nonce/token). The `random` module uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is not cryptographically secure and can be predicted if an attacker observes enough outputs.

User-controlled JSON payload is passed directly as a filter to MongoDB's find_one() without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators ($gt, $ne, $regex, etc.) to bypass query restrictions.

The MongoDB connection URL default 'mongodb://localhost:27017' contains no username, password, or authentication mechanism. If the environment variable MONGO_URL is not set, the application connects to MongoDB without any authentication, exposing the entire database.
If the MONGO_URL environment variable is not set, the code falls back to a hardcoded default MongoDB URL 'mongodb://localhost:27017' with no authentication.

The MongoDB connection URL is read from `MONGO_URL` environment variable with a default of `mongodb://localhost:27017`. If an attacker can influence this environment variable, or if the MongoDB server makes internal network requests, this could be used for SSRF. Additionally, the connection creates a new MongoClient per request, connecting to internal services.

User-controlled JSON payload is parsed and passed directly as a MongoDB query filter to `find_one()` without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like `$ne`, `$regex`, `$where` to manipulate the query logic.

The endpoint trusts the client-supplied `ops_badge` cookie (or `x-ops-badge` header) to determine if the user has elevated access ('lead'). An attacker can simply set the cookie to 'lead' to gain elevated privileges.
The `host` query parameter is directly concatenated into a shell command passed to `os.system()` without any sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands.
The same `host` parameter in the ping command allows an attacker to specify arbitrary network targets. The server will make network requests to attacker-controlled destinations or internal services.

The /ops/trace/ticket-panel-642 endpoint returns internal environment information including the APP_ENV environment variable value and the base export directory path. This leaks infrastructure details to authenticated callers.
The endpoint returns the `APP_ENV` environment variable value in the API response, exposing internal system configuration details.
PostgreSQL password is hardcoded as 'supportdesk' directly in the docker-compose configuration file. Both username and password are identical, weakening security further.
The StatusPill component renders `value` directly in JSX. However, React JSX auto-escapes by default, so this is not exploitable for XSS.
The login form pre-fills with hardcoded demo credentials (email: admin@supportdesk.local, password: DemoPass!2026) in the source code. These are also displayed in the UI at line 175-178.
